lines.text: Your microwave is slowing down your Wi-Fi.
lines.see: Tight on a phone on the kitchen counter, video frozen on a buffering spinner, the microwave glowing amber behind it

lines.text: Hit start, and the video on your phone freezes.
lines.see: Swing to the microwave keypad, START glows, back to the phone as the spinner takes over
Crane up wide over the night kitchen: router on a shelf, amber Wi-Fi packets flying to the phone past the microwave door

lines.text: A microwave cooks with radio waves at 2.45 gigahertz.
lines.see: Fly through the door into the cavity: amber waves bounce wall to wall around a turning mug, headline 2.45 GHz

lines.text: Your Wi-Fi talks at 2.4 gigahertz. Same stretch of airwaves.
lines.see: Pull out to a glowing frequency ruler in the air: the router's marker and the microwave's marker slide onto the same spot

lines.text: The metal mesh in the door blocks almost all of it.
lines.see: Push into the door: waves inside slam into the mesh and bounce back

lines.text: Its holes are a millimetre or two. The waves are twelve centimetres long.
lines.see: Extreme close on the mesh holes, one long amber wave beside them, headline 1 mm vs 12 cm

lines.text: But almost all isn't all. And your router is allowed a tenth of a watt.
lines.see: Pull back: faint amber rings leak through the door; swing to the router, headline 0.1 W

lines.text: The microwave runs on about a thousand. Even a tiny leak drowns it out.
lines.see: Headline 1,000 W counts up, wide: leak rings swell, Wi-Fi packets turn grey and drop before reaching the phone

lines.text: The fix? Put your phone on 5 gigahertz. The microwave can't touch it.
lines.see: The router's marker slides along the ruler to 5, packets switch to a high clean lane, the video plays

lines.text: So be honest. Are you on 2.4, or 5?
lines.see: Back to the same phone shot as frame 0, question headline, comment bubble

facts.claim: US rules list 2450 MHz (plus or minus 50 MHz) as an industrial, scientific and medical (ISM) frequency, the band microwave ovens use
A microwave oven's 2.45 GHz frequency gives a wavelength of about 12.2 cm; a metal mesh with holes much smaller than the wavelength blocks the waves (Swinburne University, Dr Manas Kumar Haldar)
A thin metal screen with lots of millimetre-size holes is an effective shield at 2.45 GHz (about 12.24 cm wavelength): 'wave-guide below cutoff' (University of Illinois Physics Van)

FDA: the federal standard allows ovens to leak up to 5 mW per square centimetre at about 2 inches from the surface over their lifetime, far below harmful levels; two independent interlocks are required
Apple: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi use the 2.4 GHz band; microwave ovens are listed as a common source of interference; many Wi-Fi devices can use 5 GHz instead
Microwave interference causes large degradation in Wi-Fi throughput in the 2.4 GHz band, usually worst from channel 6 to 11; fix: channel 1 or 5 GHz (CWNP, Bhaskaran Raman for AirTight Networks)
UK rules: 2.4 GHz (2400-2483.5 MHz) wideband data equipment such as Wi-Fi is limited to 100 mW e.i.r.p. (a tenth of a watt)
Household microwave ovens are rated at roughly 750 to 1,100 W (US DOE consumer guide, quoted); a typical oven magnetron is specified for 1000 W of continuous wave power at 2450 MHz
Ofcom-commissioned study (Mass Consultants, 2009) named microwave ovens among devices that can interfere with home Wi-Fi in the 2.4 GHz band

publish.caption:
It's not a myth. Microwave ovens cook at 2.45 GHz, right next to 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. The door blocks almost all of it, but a tiny legal leak is still louder than your router. 5 GHz fixes it.

2.4 or 5? 👇
